doc.title: Bernie Kirsh interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 27, 2022

chapter: Patti Smith and Return to Forever recordings
title: Recording Patti Smith's Horses
summary: Kirsh talks about the punk-rock sessions, the underground scene and the record's later honors.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: doing. And she was expressing her music via her sense of poetry and so forth, and she was working with some other musicians. But it was basically rock. It was the beginnings of punk rock. So it wasn’t something that I had been digesting at all. It was something new for me. But I got into the game of it and I was just having fun. It was just fun.

Did you ever have to go out into the main room and tell a guitar player, say, listen I can’t record you at that volume? Because I was listening to the title track and it reminded me of some of the some that I’ve been a part of in a studio here in Central New York, and I found this quote from Rolling Stone, they were talking about the date that we’re discussing and the band part of it. And this reviewer said, “The instrumental music is the kind of artful rock & roll primitism that has long characterized the New York underground.”
Did you know that at the time?
I know things were going on in the underground but I wasn’t fully aware. There were CBGBs there and there was another place on the east side that was — I’ve forgotten the name of it now but yeah.
Well the record’s become quite a historical marker I think, it’s part of the National Recording Registry for significant historical and cultural event. So it’s nice —
Yeah it just became a Grammy Hall of Fame winner as well — not winner, that’s the wrong term, I guess it’s now part of that. Yeah.
